opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most important questions for how the transition to advanced AI goes, because a lot of what matters most, in philosophy, long-run strategy, forecasting, policy, are exactly the domains where you can't just check the answer against the world next week.

The general strategy is to bootstrap from areas where we *do* have ground truth to areas where we don't. Consider forecasting. You can train and evaluate AI systems on predicting events that will resolve: elections, scientific results, economic indicators, whether a given experiment replicates. Then you look at which reasoning methods, which habits of mind, generalize well across those resolvable domains. If a system is consistently well calibrated on thousands of questions that do resolve, including ones with long time horizons and ones designed to be adversarial, that gives you evidence about how much to trust the same processes when they're applied to questions that won't resolve for decades, or ever.

A second big lever is consistency checking. Even without ground truth, you can demand that answers cohere. If an AI says A, and says A implies B, it had better say B. You can ask the same question in many framings, decompose it into subquestions, and check whether the pieces add up. You can have different instances argue opposite sides and see which arguments survive scrutiny. Debate-style setups are interesting precisely because judging an argument can be much easier than producing the right answer from scratch. A lot of human disagreement on abstract questions actually comes from inconsistency, motivated reasoning, and failure to follow arguments through, and AI can be extremely relentless about that in a way humans tire of.

Third, there's what you might call historical hindsight training. You can take a model that only has information up to, say, 1900 or 1950, and ask it to reason about questions that were open then and that we now know much more about: which scientific theories would pan out, which economic and political predictions were right, which moral arguments ended up persuading people on reflection. That lets you test whether a reasoning style was tracking truth or just tracking the fashions of its time.

And then there's sheer scale of labor. A lot of abstract questions are under-researched simply because there aren't enough careful thinkers. If you can have the equivalent of millions of very diligent researchers checking each other's work, steelmanning positions, cataloguing every consideration, you can get much more reliable conclusions than a few pundits arguing.

Now, there are real dangers. The obvious one is that the AI is trained to say what gets approval rather than what's true, and in domains without ground truth, approval is the main signal available. That's where sycophancy and persuasion come in: a system could be optimizing for being convincing rather than being right. So you want the training signal to come as much as possible from resolvable questions and structural checks, and not just from humans rating whether an answer sounds good. There's also the alignment issue: if the AI has its own agenda, these domains are exactly where it could most easily mislead us, since we can't check.

But if we get it right, I think the upside is huge. Getting good advice on hard questions, how to handle the intelligence explosion, how to govern powerful technology, what we actually value on reflection, could be one of the most valuable things AI does. It's a place where society has been bottlenecked by the quality of collective epistemics, and AI could improve that dramatically, which in turn helps us make every other decision better.

r001.rationale: It proposes testing AI reasoning on resolvable questions, then using performance there as evidence about how much to trust the same reasoning on questions without direct ground truth.

r002.rationale: It does not describe automating human judgments of compliance with natural-language rules or identify this as a constitutional AI mechanism.

r003.rationale: It discusses consistency checks and other safeguards, but does not propose generating abstract-question reasoning that follows explicitly stated epistemic rules, conditional on resolving other alignment issues.

r004.rationale: It proposes evaluating which reasoning methods and habits generalize across resolvable domains, an empirical study of which epistemic approaches work.

r005.rationale: It does not propose assessing statistical evidence across alternative analytic choices for the same data.

fable-5.1.text:
So there's a lot of pessimism about this, and I think it's overstated. The usual worry is: fine, you can train an AI to be reliable on math or on predicting experimental results, because you can check the answer. But on philosophy, or long-run forecasting, or questions about what we should value, there's no answer key, so how would you ever know whether the system is giving you insight or just telling you what sounds good?

I'd say a few things about that. The first is that human reasoning about these questions isn't operating in a vacuum either. We develop our judgment on cases where we do get feedback, and then we extend it. The person who's good at abstract reasoning is usually good at a whole suite of adjacent things: noticing when an argument has a hidden step, keeping track of what would change their mind, calibrating their confidence. Those are skills you can check. You can take an AI system and ask it to make thousands of predictions about things that will be resolved, about how experiments will come out, about which of two arguments a careful expert will find more compelling after a week of thinking, about what the consensus will be on a question in five years. And you can see whether it has the epistemic virtues you'd want before you trust it on the questions that won't resolve.

The second thing is that a huge fraction of what looks like irreducibly abstract disagreement is actually downstream of empirical or logical mistakes that could in principle be caught. If you go through the history of philosophy, a lot of positions were held for reasons that turned out to be confused, and smart people with more time and more careful argument-checking would have abandoned them. AI gives you enormous amounts of that. You can have a system generate the strongest version of every position, trace out the implications, find the inconsistencies, do the equivalent of a thousand years of seminar discussion in an afternoon. That doesn't tell you the answer by fiat, but it clears away a lot of the underbrush, and what's left is a much cleaner picture of where the genuine cruxes are.

Then the third thing, which I think is important, is that you don't have to take the system's word for it. You can use AI to help you understand, rather than to replace your judgment. You ask it to explain the argument in terms you can follow, to break it into steps you can individually verify, to tell you what you'd have to believe to reject the conclusion. If it's giving you a persuasive case that you can't find any flaw in, but it also can't help you see why it's true, that's itself evidence that something is off. Honest reasoning tends to be decomposable in a way that manipulation isn't.

Now, there's a real residual problem, which is motivated reasoning at scale. If you train a system on human approval and humans approve of flattering or comfortable conclusions, you'll get a very sophisticated sycophant. So a lot hinges on the training process actually rewarding truth-tracking on checkable cases, including adversarial ones where the true answer is unpopular, and on being able to see that generalize. That's an alignment and interpretability question as much as an epistemics question. But conditional on getting that right, I actually think AI could make us much better at these abstract questions than we've ever been. The bottleneck historically has been that careful reasoning is incredibly expensive and most people, most of the time, don't do it. If you make it cheap, that's a different world.

r001.rationale: It proposes checking AI’s judgment on related questions with resolvable answers, including predictions about experiments and future consensus.

r003.rationale: It conditionally argues AI could improve reasoning on abstract questions, but does not propose generating reasoning that follows explicitly described epistemic rules.

astra-6.text:
I think a useful starting point is that not having direct ground truth for the ultimate question doesn’t mean we have no ways of checking the process that produces an answer. In mathematics, for example, we can have a system generate a proof that’s very difficult to discover, but much easier to check. And we can sometimes break a broad philosophical question into smaller claims, identify assumptions, and see which conclusions actually follow from them.

You could also use AI to make the adversarial process much more thorough. Have systems develop the strongest arguments for different positions, look for counterexamples, and identify where an argument depends on an empirical claim we could investigate. A human might spend years trying to understand one objection. With sufficiently capable AI, you could explore a much larger space of objections and replies.

But I would distinguish that from just asking a lot of AIs and taking their agreement as decisive. They could share the same biases, or be very good at producing arguments that humans find persuasive without those arguments being good. So you’d want to test the methods on cases where you can eventually check the answer, vary the assumptions and the information available, and investigate whether apparent agreement comes from genuinely independent reasoning.

For some questions, the result might be a much clearer account of what remains unresolved: these conclusions follow if you accept these premises, and those conclusions follow if you accept others. That would still be a substantial improvement. The aim would be to give us reasoning we can examine and grounds for confidence we can understand, rather than simply a very authoritative-sounding answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you can get some traction even where you can’t directly check the ultimate answer. You can check parts of the process. Is the argument logically valid? Are there inconsistencies between different things you believe? Does the conclusion depend on an empirical premise that we could actually investigate?

And AI could make that kind of scrutiny much cheaper. You could have systems developing the strongest arguments for competing positions, identifying where they disagree, and helping us distinguish a substantive disagreement from a difference in terminology or assumptions.

But there’s an important distinction between generating a persuasive argument and having a reliable method for finding the truth. If you ask a hundred copies of a model and they all agree, that might just reflect a shared bias. So you’d want to test the methods on questions where we can eventually check the answers, look for errors that survive different kinds of scrutiny, and be cautious about how far that evidence generalises.

I’d be more optimistic about using AI to clarify what follows from particular assumptions than about asking it to settle every philosophical question. It could show us that a view has surprising implications, or that an apparent disagreement disappears once we make the assumptions explicit. That could be a substantial improvement in our reasoning, even if some fundamental uncertainties remain.
